title: Design photo sharing
dek: Zotato Snaps lets diners post photos of what they ate. Each one shows on their profile and on the restaurant's page within seconds, loads fast on a 4G phone, and survives a dish going viral.

items: Post a photo with a caption, tagged with the restaurant and dish.
See a person's photos, and a restaurant's photos, newest first, page by page.
Like a photo and see how many people liked it.
Delete your own photo; it disappears everywhere.
Out of scope here: the home feed of people you follow (that's the News feed question, 07), comments, and video.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: A grid of photos loads in about a second on a 4G phone
A new photo shows on the restaurant's page within a few seconds
A posted photo is never lost
1 crore daily users, 20 lakh new photos a day

items: Uploads: 20 lakh a day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 23 a second, maybe 100 at the dinner peak. Small for the database.
Bytes in: about 3 MB per original is 6 TB a day, roughly 2 PB a year. Object storage, not a database.
Views: 1 crore people × 50 photos seen is 50 crore a day, about 6,000 a second and 25,000 at peak. At around 100 KB each that's 2.5 GB a second: a CDN's job.
Details: 20 lakh rows a day × about 500 bytes is 1 GB a day, about 365 GB a year. One large database for a while, sharded later.
Sizes: a 20 KB thumbnail, a 150 KB feed size and a 500 KB full screen add about 0.7 MB per photo, so storing them costs a quarter of the originals but saves every phone from downloading 3 MB.
Photo: `id`, `owner_id`, `restaurant_id`, `dish`, `caption`, `created_at`, `state` (processing, live, removed), `sizes` (keys in object storage).
Restaurant photo: `restaurant_id`, `created_at`, `photo_id` (the same photos, listed by restaurant).
Like: `photo_id`, `user_id`. Like count: `photo_id`, `n`.

body.label: API

body.cap: The app gets a signed URL and uploads the original straight to object storage. Storage drops a message on a queue; a worker makes three sizes, saves them, and marks the photo live. Phones then fetch the size they need through the CDN, which reads from storage only on a miss.

body.x: The photo service never touches image bytes. It writes the record (state: processing), hands out the upload URL, and later flips the state to live when the resize worker reports back. Until then the owner sees their own photo with a "processing" badge, and nobody else sees it. A queue can deliver the same message twice, so the worker must be safe to run again: it writes each size to a fixed key, and marks the photo live only when every size exists and the content check has passed.

body.name: First try
body.what: Store the uploaded file and send it to every viewer.
body.use: Nothing to build: one file per photo.
body.avoid: A grid of 12 photos is 36 MB on a phone. Slow, expensive data for the customer, and the servers send every byte.
body.ex: A restaurant page with 12 dish photos takes 30 seconds on patchy 4G.
body.like: Mailing someone a poster when they asked for a postcard.

body.name: Better
body.what: A worker makes fixed sizes (320, 1080 and 2048 pixels wide) in a modern format, and the app asks for the one it needs.
body.use: A grid of thumbnails is about 250 KB, and the sizes are made once, not on every view.
body.avoid: Served from your own servers, 2.5 GB a second at peak still needs a lot of machines and bandwidth.
body.ex: The restaurant grid uses 320-pixel thumbnails at about 20 KB each.
body.like: A printer making postcards, posters and stamps once, then handing out the right one.

body.name: Best
body.what: Put the sizes behind a CDN with a long cache time. Give every version of a photo its own address that is never reused (the photo id and a version in the path), so it can be cached for a year without ever going stale.
body.use: Most views are answered from a server in the viewer's city; storage sees only misses.
body.avoid: Deleting a photo must also remove it from the CDN (a purge), or it lingers in caches for a while.
body.ex: A dosa photo shared in a Bengaluru food group is fetched once from storage and then served from the Bengaluru edge for everyone else.
body.like: A kirana shop stocking the popular items instead of everyone going to the warehouse.

body.x: Listing photos by person and by restaurant

items: Shard the photo table by owner, so a person's photos are in one place, sorted by `created_at`.
A restaurant's photos come from many owners, so keep a separate table keyed by `restaurant_id` with `created_at` and `photo_id`, written when a photo goes live.
Page with a cursor (the last `created_at` and `photo_id` seen), not page numbers: new photos arriving don't shift what comes next.
The two tables can disagree for a moment. Write the restaurant row from the same event that marks the photo live, and retry until it's there.

body.x: A like count for a viral photo

body.cap: One row taking every like for a viral photo becomes a queue of writers. Split the count over 8 rows: each like adds 1 to a random one, and reading the count adds the 8 up. Each row now takes an eighth of the writes.

items: A photo shared in a big group can get 50,000 likes in a few minutes, a few hundred writes a second to one row. Each waits for the one before.
Keep who liked what in the likes table (one row per person, so a double tap doesn't count twice), and the number separately.
Split the number over a few rows and add them up when reading, or count likes in memory and save the total every few seconds. Show the count from a cache; nobody minds if it's a second behind.
The resize worker also checks the image: an automated scan for unsafe content, and a person reviews anything it flags.
Remove location data before making the sizes; people don't always know their phone adds it. Keep originals in a private bucket the CDN can't reach, since they still carry it.
A deleted photo is marked removed at once, its by-restaurant row deleted, purged from the CDN, and its files deleted after a few days, in case the delete was a mistake.
Junior / mid: object storage for images, a database for details, sizes for different screens, and a CDN.
Senior: direct upload with signed URLs, a queue and resize workers, the processing state, a second table by restaurant, cursor pages.
Lead: the hot like count, moderation and privacy (location data), deletion through the CDN, and what happens when resizing falls behind at dinner.

"Resize workers fall behind at dinner." The queue absorbs it; the owner sees "processing" a little longer. Add workers based on queue length, and make the thumbnail first so the grid can show something.
"Upload fails halfway on 4G." Large files go up in parts and resume; a photo that never finished stays in processing and is cleaned up after a day.
"Same photo uploaded twice?" Hash the bytes and warn the user; don't silently merge two people's posts.
"A new screen size needs a 720-pixel version." Make it on first request at the CDN's origin and keep it, instead of reprocessing 2 PB of originals.
"How do you shard when one restaurant has a million photos?" Its rows are just more rows in the by-restaurant table; split that table by restaurant and time if one restaurant gets too big.

body.x: Serving photos is a CDN problem at heart. The IND vs PAK problem shows how much a CDN takes off your servers when everyone wants the same thing at once.
body.go: Try the IND vs PAK problem

practice.brief: Each test sends what the app does: people look at photos (each about 50 KB, the same ones again and again: a few are very popular), open a restaurant's page (its newest 30 photos), and now and then post a photo: its details go to the API, its bytes straight to storage, and thumbnails are made within five minutes.

tests.name: Post a photo
tests.desc: A diner posts a dosa photo at Thindi Mane. The API records the photo's details and hands back a signed upload link; the image itself goes straight to object storage, never through your servers.

tests.name: View a photo
tests.desc: A follower opens photo p1: the image comes from object storage (and, after the first view, from the CDN).

tests.name: Open Thindi Mane's photos
tests.desc: The newest 30 photos of restaurant r_88, newest first.

tests.name: Upload the image
tests.desc: The phone sends the image's bytes straight to object storage with the signed link.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 6,000 requests a second: photo grids and restaurant pages.

tests.name: A celebrity posts
tests.desc: At 8:10 pm a film star posts a dosa photo: photo views triple for 15 minutes.

tests.name: A zone goes dark
tests.desc: At 8:10 pm one availability zone is lost for 15 minutes. Things may slow down; posts may not be lost.

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (6,000 a second), storage and data transfer included. Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails.

wrong.name: Photos in a database table
wrong.why: The image bytes go into the rows of a table: a database is not built for big files.

wrong.name: No CDN
wrong.why: Every view reaches object storage: when a celebrity posts, it gets more requests a second than it takes.

wrong.name: No cache
wrong.why: Every restaurant page reads the database: at the peak, more than it can take.

wrong.name: Thumbnails while you wait
wrong.why: The API makes the thumbnails before answering, so posting is slow and the API servers run out.

wrong.name: One zone
wrong.why: Every API server is in one zone: when it goes dark, pages don't open.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: The database has no standby: when it crashes, pages and posts fail for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: It passes every test, at several times the bill it needs.

mutantsAllowedWhy.remove:lb: The CDN may reach the API group directly in this model.
mutantsAllowedWhy.ttl:cache: How long a page stays cached only changes how soon a new photo shows; no test asks for that.
mutantsAllowedWhy.engine:db:dynamodb: DynamoDB is an equally good store for photo details, keyed by photo with an index by restaurant.

fr.label: Post a photo with a caption, restaurant and dish
See a person's or a restaurant's photos, newest first
Like a photo and see the count

est.label: Photo views a second at peak

api.label: Create a photo (get an upload URL)

decisions.q: How does a phone upload a photo?
options: Send the bytes to the API servers, which store them
Get a signed link from the API, send bytes straight to storage
Send the bytes to the API servers, which save them in the database
decisions.why: Big uploads through app servers tie them up for seconds each, and image bytes in database rows make it huge and slow. A signed link lets object storage take the bytes while the API handles only the small details.

decisions.q: Phones on slow networks need small images. When are smaller sizes made?
options: Resized on every view, to the size the phone asks for
On the phone, after it downloads the full photo
A few sizes, once, in the background after upload
decisions.why: Resizing once is cheap; resizing on every view repeats the work crores of times, and shrinking on the phone wastes its data on the full 3 MB first.

options: A CDN in front of object storage
The app servers, reading from object storage on each view
Object storage directly, with a public link per photo
decisions.why: Popular photos are viewed again and again from all over India; a CDN answers from servers near the viewer. Serving from app servers wastes them, and object storage alone is slower and costs more per view.

hints.x: Posting, viewing, liking and deleting. Which of these happens thousands of times more than the others?
Views × image size gives bytes a second. Is that a job for your servers?
Creating a photo returns a signed upload URL; the image goes straight to object storage.
Images never change once made. Serve them from a CDN: 95% never reach you.
What still reaches your servers (page data) reads the same rows again and again: a Cache in front of the database.
A celebrity post triples photo views for 15 minutes. With a CDN in front, object storage and your servers see only the few misses.
